intro: The Talmud is full of laws. It is also full of stories. The rabbis called these stories aggadah. In this unit you will hear some of the most famous ones. A tree jumps. A stream runs backward. A voice speaks from heaven. And the rabbis still decide for themselves.

You will also meet the people behind the pages. Rabbi Akiva was a poor shepherd who began to learn late in life. His wife Rachel helped him do it. Beruriah was a learned woman whose sharp reading of a psalm is still told today. Many rabbis worked with their hands, as shoemakers and woodcutters.

By the end you will be able to retell these stories and name where they are found, like Bava Metzia 59b. You will be able to explain what each story teaches about arguing well. And you will see how the rabbis tried to be kind, even when they disagreed.
bigQuestion: What do the Talmud's stories teach about arguing well and treating people kindly?

timeline.t: Rabbi Akiva is born, tradition says, and grows up poor
The Romans destroy the Temple in Jerusalem
Rabbis gather to study at Yavneh
Rabbi Eliezer and the rabbis argue about the oven, the story says
Rabbi Akiva dies under Roman rule, after the Bar Kokhba revolt
Rabbi Meir and Beruriah teach in the Galilee
Rabbi Judah the Prince finishes the Mishnah
The Babylonian Talmud, with these stories, is completed
Students around the world still retell these stories

words.d: the stories and teachings in the Talmud that are not laws
Jewish law, the rules for how to live, as the rabbis explain them

the Mishnah together with the Gemara, the rabbis' long discussion of it

the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah, mostly in Aramaic
a teacher from the time of the Mishnah, like Rabbi Akiva or Rabbi Eliezer
a town near the sea where rabbis gathered to study after 70 CE

test.q: In the story of the oven, what were the rabbis arguing about?
choices: Whether an oven could be used and was clean
Who should lead the study house
test.why: In Bava Metzia 59b the rabbis argue whether a clay oven made of rings is clean.

test.q: Which rabbi called on a carob tree and a stream to prove him right?
test.why: Rabbi Eliezer called on the tree, the stream, the walls and a voice from heaven.

test.q: What did Rabbi Joshua mean by "It is not in heaven"?
choices: People on earth must decide the law, by majority
test.why: Rabbi Joshua used Deuteronomy 30:12 to say the Torah was given to people, who decide by majority.

test.q: Where is the story of the oven of Akhnai told?
test.why: The story is in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Bava Metzia, page 59b.

test.q: What does the word aggadah mean?
choices: The stories and teachings in the Talmud that are not laws
test.why: Aggadah is the story part of the Talmud; halakhah is the law part.

test.q: Right after the oven story, the Mishnah and Gemara warn about which hurt?
test.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 and the Gemara nearby teach against hurting people with words (ona'at devarim).

test.q: Who was Rabbi Akiva before he began to study?
test.why: The Talmud (Nedarim 50a, Ketubot 62b) tells that Akiva was a poor shepherd.

test.q: Who helped Rabbi Akiva go away to study, the Talmud says?
test.why: Ketubot 62b–63a tells that Rachel sent Akiva to study for many years.

test.q: Which verse did Rabbi Akiva call a great principle of the Torah?
test.why: Rabbi Akiva taught that Leviticus 19:18 is a great principle, as the Sifra and the Jerusalem Talmud report.

test.q: Beruriah read a psalm to teach her husband what?
choices: To pray that sins end, not that sinners die
To move to a new town
test.why: Berakhot 10a tells how Beruriah read Psalm 104:35 as a prayer for sins to end.
The Talmud names Beruriah as the wife of Rabbi Meir.

test.q: What does the Talmud show about the rabbis' jobs?
choices: Many worked with their hands, like shoemakers and woodcutters
test.why: The Talmud names rabbis who worked as a shoemaker, a woodcutter and more.

test.q: How did the rabbis decide a law when they disagreed?
choices: By what most of them said
test.why: The oven story shows the rabbis following the majority, not signs or a voice.

test.q: Why does the Talmud keep the words of a rabbi who lost an argument?
choices: So readers can still learn from the minority view
Because he won later in the story
test.why: The Talmud records minority opinions, like Rabbi Eliezer's, so they are not forgotten.

test.q: How do the stories of Akiva and Beruriah differ from the oven story?
choices: They show the rabbis as people with families and homes
test.why: The oven story is about deciding law; the Akiva and Beruriah stories show the rabbis' lives and families.

write.prompt: What do the Talmud's stories teach about disagreeing kindly? Use Bava Metzia 59b (the oven of Akhnai), Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 (hurting with words) and Berakhot 10a (Beruriah and the psalm). Say what each passage says, and how readers have understood it.
tips: Name the tractate and page for every passage you use.
Say who is speaking: "Rabbi Joshua said" or "the Talmud tells."
Tell what each story protects, like a person's feelings.
Compare two ways of reading a story instead of saying one is right.
Use the unit's words: aggadah, halakhah, majority, Talmud.
